title: Lesson 1 Quiz: Labor Supply and Demand
description: A short quiz to check what you learned in this lesson. Submitting it completes the lesson's quiz requirement, and your score is recorded separately.

history.note: AI-written question draft. Not yet reviewed by a human (admin); do not give to students.

questions.prompt: Hypothetical example: Many more people in a city start ordering meals for home delivery. What is the most likely effect on the city's labor market for delivery riders?

choices.text: Labor supply of riders shifts left, so the wage for riders falls
Labor demand for riders shifts right, so wages and employment rise
Labor demand for riders shifts left, because apps replace their work
Nothing changes, because riders do not cook the meals being ordered

questions.prompt: Hypothetical example: A juice bar is deciding whether to hire one more worker. The extra worker would let the bar sell 9 more smoothies per hour, and each smoothie sells for $4. The wage is $20 per hour. By how many dollars per hour does the value of the extra worker's output exceed the wage? (Enter a number only.)
Using the work–leisure trade-off, why does the quantity of labor supplied usually rise when the wage rises?

choices.text: Higher wages make leisure activities cheaper, so people want more free time
Employers want more workers when wages rise, which pulls people into jobs
A higher wage shifts the whole labor supply curve to the right
Each hour of leisure now means giving up more pay, so working is more attractive

questions.prompt: Hypothetical example: In a city's market for home health aides, labor demand is L_d = 1,200 − 40W and labor supply is L_s = 200 + 60W, where W is the hourly wage in dollars. How many aides are employed at the equilibrium? (Enter a number only, in workers.)

Hypothetical example: A state now requires new electricians to complete two extra years of training before they can work. Other things equal, what does the labor market model predict for electricians?

choices.text: Labor supply shifts left: the wage rises and employment falls
Labor demand shifts left: the wage falls and employment falls
Labor supply shifts right: the wage falls and employment rises
Labor demand shifts right: the wage rises and employment rises
